rationale: A wins because it keeps its hands where the facts are. "The number Toast won't give you: default rates on its restaurant cash advances" is a real accountability angle, and A immediately names the proof that could kill it. B has useful instincts, but "Toast got profitable by selling money, not hardware" turns a margin clue into an unsupported causal headline. That is how a pitch gets interesting and wrong at the same time.
gaps_in_A: A wrongly throws away a viable labor-ops angle: "Toast payroll solves the tipped-vs-hourly staffing headache for operators" is not a duplicate of the borrowing/customer story; payroll for tipped and hourly staff is a separate restaurant-trade beat if backed by an operator.

A's next step is too procedural and too dismissive: "there is no live news signal in this update" ignores that bundling, profitability, and the 120,000-location milestone are enough of a current peg for targeted outreach if the proof exists.
A misses the incumbent-finance foil that could sharpen the lending story: community banks, small-business lenders, or merchant-cash-advance regulators are not protagonists anywhere in the kept set.
gaps_in_B: B overclaims causation in "Toast got profitable by selling money, not hardware"; the update says Toast recently reached profitability and says fintech is higher-margin, not that lending caused profitability.

B invents substitution in "Restaurants are borrowing from their point-of-sale system instead of their bank"; the facts say Toast offers cash advances, not that restaurants are choosing Toast over banks.
B smuggles in an underwriting claim: "underwritten by the payment flow Toast already sees" may be plausible, but it is not in the update and needs confirmation before it becomes copy.

B pads the payroll angle with outside assumptions: "tip pooling, wage credits, variable shifts" may be real restaurant payroll problems, but the supplied fact only says the product targets tipped and hourly staff. Useful color, not grounded proof.
